argument: For broad classes of stable feedback loops, reducing sensitivity $|S(j\omega)|$ over one frequency range requires increased sensitivity elsewhere, especially with unstable poles, delays, or nonminimum-phase zeros. Feedback performance has a waterbed trade-off.
boundary: Exact integrals depend on plant stability, properness, delays, and loop assumptions.
Nonlinear or time-varying control requires other bounds.
Shaping disturbances and noise can move the practical optimum.
claim: For broad classes of stable feedback loops, reducing sensitivity $|S(j\omega)|$ over one frequency range requires increased sensitivity elsewhere, especially with unstable poles, delays, or nonminimum-phase zeros. Feedback performance has a waterbed trade-off.
interpretation: Claims of simultaneous disturbance rejection, fast response, low noise, and robustness should be checked against fundamental trade-offs.

argument: Clinical outcomes are produced by biological states filtered through diagnostic criteria, instruments, coding, healthcare access, and surveillance intensity. Changing a case definition or ascertainment process can create apparent incidence, prevalence, severity, or treatment-effect changes without equivalent biological change.
boundary: Some diseases have highly specific objective markers; others are syndromic or spectrum-based.
Differential measurement by treatment, site, or subgroup can create bias.
Harmonization can improve comparability but may discard clinically relevant local detail.
claim: Clinical outcomes are produced by biological states filtered through diagnostic criteria, instruments, coding, healthcare access, and surveillance intensity. Changing a case definition or ascertainment process can create apparent incidence, prevalence, severity, or treatment-effect changes without equivalent biological change.
interpretation: Principia should store the case definition and its version as part of a Principle’s scope. Label quality is not merely a preprocessing detail.

argument: In systems with interactive complexity and tight coupling, local failures can combine through unexpected pathways faster than operators can diagnose or isolate them. Some accidents are therefore emergent consequences of system organization rather than simple violations by one component or person.
boundary: The theory does not imply that every complex system is unmanageable.
Modularity, slack, transparency, and decoupling can reduce risk.
Empirical classification of “normal” accidents remains debated.
